claims.text: The extent of local chemical ordering governs the structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic high-entropy nanoparticles under service conditions.
Homogeneous mixing of multiple elements produces enhanced local chemical ordering.
Local chemical ordering creates a rugged energy landscape.
The rugged energy landscape associated with local chemical ordering slows atomic diffusion.
Sluggish diffusion reduces high-temperature phase segregation and sintering.
Rapid synthesis can produce near-equiatomic, multi-element nanoparticles.
Rapidly synthesized nanoparticles have a relatively randomized chemical structure with minimal local chemical ordering.
Moderate-temperature post-synthesis annealing promotes local chemical ordering.
The annealing intervention is intended to leave the overall alloy composition unchanged.
Local chemical ordering produces heterogeneous bonding and lattice strain that impede atomic mobility.
Enhanced local chemical ordering increases activation barriers for atomic movement.
Increasing atomic-movement barriers preserves a single-phase, chemically homogeneous nanoparticle structure by mitigating segregation and sintering.
Annealed, local-order-enhanced nanoparticles will exhibit less phase separation than unannealed nanoparticles after thermal service.
Annealed, local-order-enhanced nanoparticles will retain greater compositional homogeneity after thermal service.
Annealed nanoparticles will retain higher catalytic or thermoelectric performance than unannealed nanoparticles.
Unannealed, randomly ordered nanoparticles undergo phase segregation, diffusion-driven compositional change, and functional degradation during high-temperature service.
Very high noble-metal content may alter diffusion kinetics enough to place the material outside the hypothesis's domain.
The proposed stabilization may fail when service temperatures greatly exceed the relevant diffusion-barrier thresholds.
